h1.en: Does a copper peptide serum reduce wrinkles?

byline.en: Appraised by the Skingenetix research team. Medically reviewed by Dr Esther Bodde, Cosmetic & Medical Physician. Last reviewed 24 September 2026.

verdict.en: **Our verdict:** this is the strongest controlled human trial we have for copper peptide, and it is why GHK-Cu is in our range. But the base it was measured against lacked the nano-carrier as well as the peptide, and the paper never states a concentration — so the result belongs to the serum that was tested, not to ours.

Against the plain serum vehicle the GHK-Cu side fell further — volume −24.1% against −15.0%, depth −20.3% against −15.3% — which the paper reports as a 55.8% greater reduction in volume (p < 0.0001) and 32.8% in depth (p = 0.0123). body.en: Forty women applied a GHK-Cu serum to the right side of the face twice a day for eight weeks. On the left side, half of them used a product containing Matrixyl 3000 and half used the plain serum base. Neither the women nor the investigators knew which product was which.
A separate arm of the same paper grew human skin cells with GHK-Cu and measured collagen and elastin production, which is where the paper’s laboratory findings come from.

items.en: What was compared. The GHK-Cu serum was tested against the same base without the peptide and without the lipid nano-carrier that delivered it, so the 55.8% belongs to the peptide and its delivery system together. The authors describe it as the first trial of GHK-Cu formulated into a nano-carrier.
How it relates to our products. Our formulas state 2% GHK-Cu on the pack and do not use that nano-carrier, so the figure describes the serum that was tested rather than ours.
Concentration. The paper does not report how much GHK-Cu the tested serum contained, so the result is not tied to a percentage.
Which side was treated. The GHK-Cu serum always went on the right side of the face and the comparator on the left; the sides were not randomised.
Against a Matrixyl 3000 product. The GHK-Cu side reduced wrinkle volume 31.6% more (p = 0.0044). The difference in depth was smaller and did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.0577).
Scale and funding. One trial of 39 women at a cosmetic research institute, funded by Snowberry New Zealand Ltd, which makes the serum, and published in the Journal of Aging Science.

heading.en: What it means for our products

body.en: This is the strongest controlled human trial we have for copper peptide, and it is why GHK-Cu appears in our range at all. But the serum it tested is not ours: it used a lipid nano-carrier and never disclosed its concentration.

So we cite it as evidence for the ingredient, not as a result our products have reproduced. Our own [copper peptide serum](https://www.skingenetix.com/products/copper-peptide-ghk-cu-renewal-serum), day gel-cream and night cream each state 2% GHK-Cu on the pack, which this trial cannot confirm or contradict. The rest of the evidence for the ingredient is set out on the [copper peptide research hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/copper-peptide-research).

answer.en: The Badenhorst 2016 trial is a randomised, double-blind, split-face study of a copper peptide (GHK-Cu) serum in 40 women aged 40 to 65. Over 8 weeks, wrinkle volume on the treated side fell 24.1%, against 15.0% on the plain serum base — a 55.8% greater reduction, measured by 3D imaging.

definition.en: Copper peptide, or GHK-Cu, is a chain of three amino acids — glycine, histidine and lysine — bound to a copper ion. It occurs naturally in human blood, where it was first isolated in 1973, and its level falls with age: from about 200 ng/mL at 20 to 80 ng/mL by 60.

heading.en: What copper peptide is, and where this trial sits

body.en: In skincare, GHK-Cu is used to support the look of firmer, smoother skin. In laboratory work it raises the collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycans that skin cells produce, and a review by the scientist who first isolated GHK sets out that role in detail ([Pickart et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26236730/)). Evidence in actual skin is thinner: a 2026 systematic review in *Aesthetic Surgery Journal* found GHK-Cu significantly reduced wrinkle volume and depth against controls, but drew on only **two** controlled trials among twenty studies, and said its findings were limited by methodological variability ([Mokhtar et al., 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42619529/)).

This page appraises the stronger of those two trials. It is the reason GHK-Cu is in our range, and it is also the reason we do not claim more than an ingredient-level result. The full picture — every study we rely on, graded — is on the [copper peptide evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/copper-peptide-research), which sits alongside our other [ingredient research](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/the-science).

answers.en: It shows that a GHK-Cu serum reduced the volume of one wrinkle near the eye 55.8% more than a plain serum base in 20 women (p < 0.0001), and 31.6% more than a commercial Matrixyl 3000 product in 19 others (p = 0.0044), measured by 3D imaging over 8 weeks; against the Matrixyl product the depth difference was smaller (p = 0.0577). The plain base lacked the nano-carrier as well as the peptide, so the result belongs to the two together. It is one trial, funded by the serum's maker ([Badenhorst et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.4172/2329-8847.1000166)); the other trials we rely on are on the [evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/copper-peptide-research).

The paper never states one. That is why no claim on this site says a result was “clinically proven at 2%” — the trial cannot support a concentration claim, and our own products state 2% GHK-Cu on the pack independently of it.

Partly. It was run at Dermatest GmbH, a cosmetic research institute, and the statistics were done at the University of Auckland. But it was funded by Snowberry New Zealand Ltd, which makes the serum that was tested, and it was published in a journal whose peer review is weaker than the major dermatology titles. We grade it A− for those reasons.

No, and we do not claim they do. The serum tested here used a lipid nano-carrier that our formulas do not, and its concentration was never disclosed. We cite this trial as evidence for the ingredient, not as a result our products have repeated.

heading.en: What the trial found, result by result

title.en: Crow's-feet wrinkle volume fell 55.8% more than with the plain serum

body.en: Wrinkle volume is the space a crease takes up below the surrounding skin. After a skin check and ten days without cosmetics, each woman had one large wrinkle chosen close to the corner of the eye, where crow's feet form, and that same wrinkle was measured in 3D at the start and after 8 weeks. In this group of 20 women the GHK-Cu serum went on the right side of the face and the plain serum on the left, morning and evening, with no other skincare on those areas.

By week 8, wrinkle volume on the GHK-Cu side was down 24.1% from the start, against 15.0% on the plain side: a 55.8% greater reduction (p < 0.0001), the clearest result in the trial. The paper adds that every participant using the GHK-Cu serum, in both groups, showed a reduction in wrinkle volume and depth.

Because both sides belong to the same face, differences between women drop out of the comparison, and the gap reflects what was applied. For anyone with crow's feet it is the most relevant number in the paper, measured on exactly that line. The plain serum carried neither the GHK-Cu nor the lipid nano-carrier that delivered it, so the extra reduction belongs to the two together ([Badenhorst et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.4172/2329-8847.1000166)).

result.en: Volume −24.1% vs −15.0% with the plain serum

title.en: Wrinkle volume fell 31.6% more than with a Matrixyl 3000 product

body.en: The other 19 women put the GHK-Cu serum on the right side and a commercial skincare product containing Matrixyl 3000 on the left. Matrixyl 3000 is a peptide ingredient already used in commercial skincare, and it includes a fat-soluble form of GHK; the researchers chose it as a positive control, a comparison expected to improve wrinkles too. Both products came in identical coded containers, so neither the women nor the investigators knew which was which.

After 8 weeks, wrinkle volume on the GHK-Cu side was down 25.8% from the start, against 20.0% on the Matrixyl side: a 31.6% greater reduction (p = 0.0044). At 4 weeks the two sides had improved by almost the same amount (17.2% and 16.8%). The GHK-Cu side pulled ahead in the second month, when its reduction grew by about half again while the Matrixyl side's grew by about a fifth.

Beating another active product is a harder test than beating a plain base. The timing matters too for anyone starting a GHK-Cu serum: in this trial the larger gains came between weeks 4 and 8, so the first month is not the whole story ([Badenhorst et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.4172/2329-8847.1000166)).

title.en: Wrinkle depth fell 32.8% more than with the plain serum

body.en: Depth is how far the crease sinks below the surrounding skin. PRIMOS, the 3D imaging system used here, measures it without touching the face: it projects a pattern of fine parallel stripes onto the skin, a camera records how the stripes bend over the crease, and software turns that bending into a three-dimensional map. The woman's head is held still in a support while the measuring head is brought close.

In the 20 women who compared the GHK-Cu serum with the plain serum, the same wrinkle was 20.3% shallower on the GHK-Cu side after 8 weeks, against 15.3% on the plain side: a 32.8% greater reduction (p = 0.0123).

Depth and volume are two readings of the same line, and on both the GHK-Cu side came out ahead of the plain serum. Together they describe a crow's-feet wrinkle that became both shallower and smaller over the eight weeks ([Badenhorst et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.4172/2329-8847.1000166)).

heading.en: How does GHK-Cu work on skin?

title.en: Skin cells made up to 18% more collagen in the laboratory

body.en: In the laboratory arm of the same paper, the researchers grew fibroblasts from adult human skin: the cells that make collagen, the protein that gives skin its firm framework. They added GHK-Cu at three very low strengths (0.01, 1 and 100 nanomolar, a ten-thousand-fold range), gave a matching set of cells water only, and measured the collagen the cells released into the surrounding fluid.

By day 4, the cells given GHK-Cu had released 9% to 18% more collagen than the untreated cells, at every strength (p < 0.05), and the weakest strength gave the largest rise. The researchers give these laboratory findings as the reason they went on to test the serum on faces ([Badenhorst et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.4172/2329-8847.1000166)).

title.en: Skin cells built about 30% more elastin in the laboratory

body.en: Elastin is the stretchy protein that lets skin spring back into shape. In the same laboratory experiment, the researchers also measured the elastin the fibroblasts had built up, using a colour test that reads elastin once it has been made soluble.

After 2 days the difference was small; by day 4 the cells given GHK-Cu held about 30% more elastin than the untreated cells, at every strength (29% to 35%, p < 0.017), with no clear difference between strengths. It is a laboratory finding that helps explain how GHK-Cu may work, while the trial on faces measured the wrinkle itself ([Badenhorst et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.4172/2329-8847.1000166)).
